claim: Calyculin (1 µM) strongly prolonged the decay of PTP at the calyx of Held synapse.
source: Acute application of calyculin (1 µM), an inhibitor of phosphatases PP1 and PP2A (Ishihara et al., 1989), strongly prolonged the decay of PTP (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of calyculin on PTP decay, as shown in Figure 1A and quantified in the text.

claim: The PTP decay rate was slowed from 16.0 ± 2.6%/min to 4.04 ± 1.7%/min by calyculin.
source: We estimated the decay rate of PTP by line fits (Figure 1A, grey and red line), and found that the PTP decay rate was slowed from 16.0 ± 2.6%/min to 4.04 ± 1.7%/min (Figure 1B; n = 7 cells; p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Calyculin did not change the baseline synaptic strength.
source: Calyculin acted without changing the baseline synaptic strength (Figure 1A,C; p=0.96), nor the peak PTP amplitude (219 ± 17% and 227 ± 17%, in control and calyculin respectively; p=0.7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements showing no significant difference in baseline synaptic strength.

claim: Calyculin did not change the peak PTP amplitude.
source: Calyculin acted without changing the baseline synaptic strength (Figure 1A,C; p=0.96), nor the peak PTP amplitude (219 ± 17% and 227 ± 17%, in control and calyculin respectively; p=0.7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements showing no significant difference in peak PTP amplitude.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio was decreased during the peak of PTP under control conditions.
source: Under control conditions, the paired-pulse ratio was decreased during the peak of PTP, and then recovered when PTP decayed back to baseline (Figure 1D, black data points).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The decreased paired-pulse ratio confirms that PTP is presynaptic in origin and mediated by increased transmitter release.
source: The decreased paired-pulse ratio confirms the view that PTP is presynaptic in origin, and mediated by an increased transmitter release (Habets and Borst, 2005; Korogod et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the paired-pulse ratio data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the presence of calyculin, both the decay of PTP and the recovery of the paired pulse ratio were slowed.
source: In the presence of calyculin both the decay of PTP as well as the recovery of the paired pulse ratio were slowed, revealing a parallel regulation of both the synaptic strength and the paired-pulse ratio by calyculin (Figure 1D; red data points; n = 7 cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Following PTP induction trains, the mEPSC frequency was increased and then relaxed back to baseline value over several tens of seconds.
source: Following the PTP induction trains, we found that the mEPSC frequency was increased and then relaxed back to baseline value over several tens of seconds, as shown before (Korogod et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Under control conditions, the mEPSC amplitude was increased by 23% on average during the first 10 s interval following PTP induction.
source: Under control conditions, the mEPSC amplitude was increased during the first 10 s interval following PTP induction (by 23% on average; Figure 1F; p<0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In the presence of calyculin, the elevated mEPSC frequency following PTP induction trains did not recover completely but persisted at 2–3-fold elevated levels.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of calyculin, the elevated mEPSC frequency following PTP induction trains did not recover completely, but rather, persisted at 2–3-fold elevated levels (Figure 1E, bottom). This effect was observed in all cells in which mEPSC frequency was analyzed (n = 5; p<0.001; Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: PKC inhibitory peptide (PKCi) strongly suppressed PTP at the calyx of Held synapse.
source: PKCi strongly suppressed PTP (Figure 2A,B; p<0.001), whereas PTP was normal in the presence of PKAi (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: PTP was normal in the presence of PKA inhibitory peptide (PKAi).
source: PKCi strongly suppressed PTP (Figure 2A,B; p<0.001), whereas PTP was normal in the presence of PKAi (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no effect of PKAi on PTP.

claim: The baseline synaptic strength was similar in the presence of PKCi and PKAi.
source: The baseline synaptic strength was similar under both conditions (Figure 2C; p=0.92).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements showing no significant difference.

claim: The phospholipase C inhibitor U73122 (3 µM) did not have significant effects on PTP.
source: Therefore, we tested the role of the phospholipase C inhibitor U73122 (3 µM), but we could not find significant effects on PTP (Figure 2E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no significant effect.

claim: Neomycin (10 µM) did not suppress PTP.
source: Similarly, another PLC inhibitor Neomycin (10 µM) did not suppress PTP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), despite an immediate effect of Neomycin on transmitter release, which was probably caused by inhibition of presynaptic P/Q-type Ca2+ channels (Pichler et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation explaining the side effect of Neomycin.

claim: Expression of Cre recombinase in VCN neurons of Munc18-1lox/lox mice essentially abolished depolarization-evoked release at the calyx of Held synapse.
source: When we expressed Cre recombinase in VCN neurons of Munc18-1lox/lox mice using a GFP-IRES-Cre expression cassette (Figure 3A2), depolarization-evoked release at the calyx of Held synapse was essentially abolished (Figure 3B2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of Cre-mediated Munc18-1 deletion.

claim: Control experiments with a GFP expressing virus in Munc18-1lox/lox mice showed normal depolarization-evoked EPSCs.
source: In contrast, control experiments with a GFP expressing virus (Figure 3A1) in Munc18-1lox/lox mice showed normal depolarization-evoked EPSCs (Figure 3B1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental control data.

claim: EPSCs were 0.251 ± 0.199 nA when presynaptic neurons expressed GFP-IRES-Cre and 11.2 ± 1.0 nA when expressing GFP.
source: On average, EPSCs were 0.251 ± 0.199 nA (n = 6 cells) and 11.2 ± 1.0 nA (n = 3 cells) when presynaptic neurons expressed GFP-IRES-Cre and GFP respectively (Figure 3C; p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The amplitude of presynaptic Ca2+ currents was unchanged by Cre-mediated Munc18-1 deletion.
source: The amplitude of presynaptic Ca2+ currents was unchanged under both conditions (1.07 ± 0.20 and 1.08 ± 0.08 nA for GFP-IRES-Cre and GFP respectively; see also Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements showing no significant difference.

claim: Munc18-1 is necessary for vesicle fusion, but not for presynaptic Ca2+ channel function.
source: In all cases, presynaptic Ca2+ currents were unchanged (Figure 3B,D; p>0.05), which suggests that Munc18-1 is necessary for vesicle fusion, but not for presynaptic Ca2+ channel function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing unchanged Ca2+ currents despite abolished release.

claim: Simultaneous re-expression of Munc18-1 protein together with Cre recombinase and GFP led to nearly complete rescue of the Munc18-1 k.o. release phenotype.
source: We next wished to test whether the simultaneous re-expression of Munc18-1 protein, together with the expression of Cre recombinase and GFP in the three-protein expression construct (Figure 3A3), would lead to efficient rescue of the Munc18-1 k.o. release phenotype. Indeed, depolarization-evoked release responses were nearly completely rescued (6.7 ± 2.3 nA, n = 5; Figure 3B3,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of release function.

claim: Virus injections early postnatally at P1 were necessary for complete removal of Munc18-1 function.
source: Additional experiments showed that virus injections early postnatally at P1 were necessary for complete removal of Munc18-1 function (Figure 3—Figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The mutant and wild-type forms of Munc18-1 produced baseline EPSCs of similar amplitudes.
source: The mutant and wild-type forms of Munc18-1 produced baseline EPSCs of similar amplitudes (2.87 ± 0.59 nA and 2.91 ± 0.61 nA respectively; p=0.96; Figure 4B1–D1,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data showing no significant difference.

claim: M18WT-synapses showed normal PTP of 221 ± 15% of baseline EPSC amplitude.
source: While M18WT-synapses showed normal PTP of 221 ± 15% of baseline EPSC amplitude (n = 12; see Figure 4B1 for an example), synapses rescued with the Munc18SA mutant showed significantly smaller PTP (147 ± 13% of baseline; n = 15; p<0.001; Figure 4B1–D1,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data.

claim: Synapses rescued with the Munc18SA mutant showed significantly smaller PTP (147 ± 13% of baseline).
source: While M18WT-synapses showed normal PTP of 221 ± 15% of baseline EPSC amplitude (n = 12; see Figure 4B1 for an example), synapses rescued with the Munc18SA mutant showed significantly smaller PTP (147 ± 13% of baseline; n = 15; p<0.001; Figure 4B1–D1,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The cumulative PTP attained at 150 s was 5.06 ± 1.17 in M18WT and 0.83 ± 0.85 in M18SA-rescued synapses.
source: The cumulative PTP attained at 150 s was 5.06 ± 1.17 and 0.83 ± 0.85 (unit, fold change −1) in M18WT and M18SA-rescued synapses, respectively (n = 12 and 13, respectively; p<0.01).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Replacing endogenous Munc18-1 protein by a PKC-deficient mutant selectively impaired the potentiation of evoked release during PTP.
source: Taken together, replacing endogenous Munc18-1 protein by a PKC-deficient mutant selectively impaired the potentiation of evoked release during PTP, whereas the baseline transmitter release was unaffected, and late asynchronous release depended only marginally on PKC phosphorylation of Munc18-1.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Munc18-1 is an important target protein for PKC phosphorylation during PTP.
source: These experiments show that Munc18-1 is an important target protein for PKC phosphorylation during PTP.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the gene replacement experiments showing the requirement of Munc18-1 phosphorylation sites for PTP.

claim: The phorbol ester PDBu (1 µM) potentiated EPSCs in calyx synapses rescued with M18SA, but the potentiation was about twofold smaller than with Munc18WT.
source: The phorbol ester PDBu (1 µM) still potentiated EPSCs in calyx synapses rescued with M18SA, but the potentiation was significantly, about twofold smaller than with Munc18WT (157 ± 10% of control and 202 ± 18% of control, respectively; p<0.05; Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The frequency of spontaneous mEPSCs was potentiated by phorbol ester, but the potentiation was smaller in synapses rescued with M18SA compared to M18WT.
source: Similarly, the frequency of spontaneous mEPSCs was potentiated by phorbol ester, but the potentiation was again smaller in synapses rescued with M18SA as compared to synapses expressing M18WT (307 ± 41% vs 518 ± 50%, respectively; p<0.05, Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: PKC phosphorylation of Munc18-1 accounts for part of the potentiation of evoked- and spontaneous release by phorbol esters.
source: We conclude that PKC phosphorylation of Munc18-1 accounts for part of the potentiation of evoked- and spontaneous release by phorbol esters.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing partial reduction of phorbol ester effects in M18SA synapses.

claim: A dynamic phosphorylation/de-phosphorylation cycle of Munc18-1, initiated by PKC activity, causes PTP.
source: Together, these results show that a dynamic phosphorylation/de-phosphorylation cycle of Munc18-1, initiated by PKC activity, causes PTP.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the pharmacological and genetic experiments presented in the study.

claim: Conventional PKC isoforms α and β are involved in PTP at the calyx synapse.
source: A membrane-permeable peptide inhibitor of conventional PKC isoforms α and β suppressed PTP, whereas a similar PKA inhibitor had no effect (Figure 2). The peptide inhibitors have a more defined PKC isoform specificity than the synthetic PKC inhibitors used earlier (Brager et al., 2003; Korogod et al., 2007). This, together with recent findings from knock-out mouse lines (Fioravante et al., 2011), allows us to conclude that during PTP induction stimuli, conventional PKC isoforms are activated.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data with peptide inhibitors and supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Novel PKCs, including PKCε, are unlikely to play a major role during PTP.
source: Although we cannot exclude that PKCε contributes to phorbol ester potentiation of release, it seems unlikely that novel PKCs, including PKCε, play a major role during PTP, a conclusion which agrees with the inefficiency of PLC inhibitors (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing inefficiency of PLC inhibitors.

claim: Munc18-1 is not phosphorylated in the nerve terminal under baseline conditions.
source: This indicates that Munc18-1 is not phosphorylated in the nerve terminal under baseline conditions; a conclusion which agrees with previous work using a synaptosome preparation (de Vries et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of baseline changes in various experimental manipulations and supported by a citation.

claim: During or shortly after high-frequency activity, Munc18-1 is phosphorylated by a conventional PKC isoform, which induces short-term enhancement of release.
source: Therefore, it seems likely that during, or shortly after high-frequency activity, Munc18-1 is phosphorylated by a conventional PKC isoform, which induces short-term enhancement of release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing the requirement of PKC and Munc18-1 phosphorylation for PTP.

claim: About a minute after high-frequency activity, a phosphatase de-phosphorylates Munc18-1, which terminates the enhanced evoked release during PTP.
source: About a minute later, a phosphatase de-phosphorylates Munc18-1, which terminates the enhanced evoked release during PTP.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the calyculin experiments showing prolonged PTP when phosphatases are blocked.

claim: About half of the phorbol ester potentiation of spontaneous release at the calyx synapse depends on an intact DAG binding site of Munc13-1.
source: Indeed, we have shown previously that ∼half of the phorbol ester potentiation of spontaneous release at the calyx synapse depended on an intact DAG binding site of Munc13-1 (Lou et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Phorbol ester activates at least two parallel signaling pathways at the release machinery: Munc13-1 via direct binding to its C1 domain, and PKC which then phosphorylates Munc18-1.
source: Thus, phorbol ester activates at least two parallel signaling pathways at the release machinery: on the one hand, Munc13-1 via direct binding to its C1 domain (Betz et al., 1998; Rhee et al., 2002; Lou et al., 2008), and on the other hand PKC which then phosphorylates Munc18-1 (Figure 5; Wierda et al., 2007; see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the current experimental data and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Various protein phosphatases and conventional PKCs are enriched at short distances to P/Q-type and N-type Ca2+ channels.
source: Indeed, a recent proteomics study showed that various protein phosphatases and conventional PKCs are enriched at short distances to P/Q-type and N-type Ca2+ channels (Müller et al., 2010), indicating a PKC–protein phosphatase signaling complex at the active zone.
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a proteomics study.

claim: Munc18-1 binds to the SNARE complex.
source: However, it was shown later that Munc18-1 also binds to the SNARE complex (Dulubova et al., 2007), and stimulates SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion in a reconstituted system, by binding to the partially assembled SNARE complex (Shen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc18-1 likely remains present at the partially formed SNARE complexes of docked and readily releasable vesicles.
source: Therefore, Munc18-1 likely remains present at the partially formed SNARE complexes of docked and readily releasable vesicles; interestingly, Munc13-1 is also present in this complex (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from previous studies and supported by a citation.

claim: PKC phosphorylation of Munc18-1 increases the release probability of readily releasable vesicles in a 'post-priming' regulatory step of vesicle fusion.
source: In this model, PKC phosphorylation of Munc18-1 would then increase the release probability of readily releasable vesicles, in what appears a 'post-priming' regulatory step of vesicle fusion (see schematic in Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is a speculative model based on the experimental findings and previous knowledge.

claim: Phorbol esters induce a shift and a decreased slope in the dose–response curve between transmitter release rate and presynaptic Ca2+ concentration.
source: It was shown that phorbol esters induce a shift and a decreased slope in the dose–response curve between transmitter release rate and presynaptic Ca2+ concentration (Lou et al., 2005); this modulation was reduced by PKC inhibitors (Korogod et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: PTP is not observed during presynaptic whole-cell recordings.
source: We could not apply Ca2+ uncaging to study PTP, since PTP is not observed during presynaptic whole-cell recordings (Korogod et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc18-1 is essential for vesicle fusion at synapses.
source: Munc18-1 is essential for vesicle fusion at synapses (Figure 3; Verhage et al., 2000), and Munc18-1 is expressed widely in the brain (Website, 2012; Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc18-1 is expressed widely in the brain.
source: Munc18-1 is essential for vesicle fusion at synapses (Figure 3; Verhage et al., 2000), and Munc18-1 is expressed widely in the brain (Website, 2012; Lein et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies and databases.

claim: A long-lasting residual Ca2+ signal, caused by mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake and release mechanisms, is important for short-term enhancement of release including PTP.
source: A long-lasting residual Ca2+ signal, caused by mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake and release mechanisms, is important for short-term enhancement of release including PTP (Kamiya and Zucker, 1994; Regehr et al., 1994; Tang and Zucker, 1997; Habets and Borst, 2005; Korogod et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Munc18-1 has two consensus sites for PKC phosphorylation.
source: Munc18-1 has two consensus sites for PKC phosphorylation (Fujita et al., 1996) which become phosphorylated during depolarization of synaptosomes (de Vries et al., 2000), and which are necessary for phorbol ester potentiation of transmitter release in cultured neurons (Wierda et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: The PKC phosphorylation sites of Munc18-1 become phosphorylated during depolarization of synaptosomes.
source: Munc18-1 has two consensus sites for PKC phosphorylation (Fujita et al., 1996) which become phosphorylated during depolarization of synaptosomes (de Vries et al., 2000), and which are necessary for phorbol ester potentiation of transmitter release in cultured neurons (Wierda et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: The PKC phosphorylation sites of Munc18-1 are necessary for phorbol ester potentiation of transmitter release in cultured neurons.
source: Munc18-1 has two consensus sites for PKC phosphorylation (Fujita et al., 1996) which become phosphorylated during depolarization of synaptosomes (de Vries et al., 2000), and which are necessary for phorbol ester potentiation of transmitter release in cultured neurons (Wierda et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: PTP has been shown to be sensitive to pharmacological inhibition of PKC.
source: PTP has been shown to be sensitive to pharmacological inhibition of PKC (Alle et al., 2001; Brager et al., 2003; Korogod et al., 2007), and deletion of the PKC α and β genes in mice suppressed PTP at the calyx synapse (Fioravante et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of the PKC α and β genes in mice suppressed PTP at the calyx synapse.
source: PTP has been shown to be sensitive to pharmacological inhibition of PKC (Alle et al., 2001; Brager et al., 2003; Korogod et al., 2007), and deletion of the PKC α and β genes in mice suppressed PTP at the calyx synapse (Fioravante et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous genetic study.

claim: Calyculin is an inhibitor of phosphatases PP1 and PP2A.
source: Acute application of calyculin (1 µM), an inhibitor of phosphatases PP1 and PP2A (Ishihara et al., 1989), strongly prolonged the decay of PTP (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study characterizing calyculin.

claim: Transmitter release at synapses is regulated by preceding neuronal activity.
source: Transmitter release at synapses is regulated by preceding neuronal activity, which can give rise to short-term enhancement of release like post-tetanic potentiation (PTP).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about synaptic plasticity.

claim: Diacylglycerol (DAG) and Protein-kinase C (PKC) signaling in the nerve terminal have been widely implicated in the short-term modulation of transmitter release.
source: Diacylglycerol (DAG) and Protein-kinase C (PKC) signaling in the nerve terminal have been widely implicated in the short-term modulation of transmitter release, but the target protein of PKC phosphorylation during short-term enhancement has remained unknown.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge from previous research.

claim: Two PKC phosphorylation sites of Munc18-1 are critically important for PTP.
source: We find that two PKC phosphorylation sites of Munc18-1 are critically important for PTP, which identifies the presynaptic target protein for the action of PKC during PTP.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding supported by the gene replacement experiments.

claim: PTP is initiated by the action of a 'conventional' PKC isoform.
source: Pharmacological experiments show that a phosphatase normally limits the duration of PTP, and that PTP is initiated by the action of a 'conventional' PKC isoform.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the pharmacological findings with PKC inhibitory peptides.

claim: A phosphatase normally limits the duration of PTP.
source: Pharmacological experiments show that a phosphatase normally limits the duration of PTP, and that PTP is initiated by the action of a 'conventional' PKC isoform.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the findings with calyculin showing prolonged PTP when phosphatases are blocked.

claim: PTP has been observed at excitatory synapses in hippocampus.
source: The other common form of short-term enhancement, PTP, has been observed at excitatory synapses in hippocampus (McNaughton, 1982; Lee et al., 2007), cerebellum (Beierlein et al., 2007), calyx of Held brainstem synapses (Habets and Borst, 2005; Korogod et al., 2005) and at the neuromuscular junction (Magleby and Zengel, 1975).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: PTP has been observed at excitatory synapses in cerebellum.
source: The other common form of short-term enhancement, PTP, has been observed at excitatory synapses in hippocampus (McNaughton, 1982; Lee et al., 2007), cerebellum (Beierlein et al., 2007), calyx of Held brainstem synapses (Habets and Borst, 2005; Korogod et al., 2005) and at the neuromuscular junction (Magleby and Zengel, 1975).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: PTP has been observed at calyx of Held brainstem synapses.
source: The other common form of short-term enhancement, PTP, has been observed at excitatory synapses in hippocampus (McNaughton, 1982; Lee et al., 2007), cerebellum (Beierlein et al., 2007), calyx of Held brainstem synapses (Habets and Borst, 2005; Korogod et al., 2005) and at the neuromuscular junction (Magleby and Zengel, 1975).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: PTP has been observed at the neuromuscular junction.
source: The other common form of short-term enhancement, PTP, has been observed at excitatory synapses in hippocampus (McNaughton, 1982; Lee et al., 2007), cerebellum (Beierlein et al., 2007), calyx of Held brainstem synapses (Habets and Borst, 2005; Korogod et al., 2005) and at the neuromuscular junction (Magleby and Zengel, 1975).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: Studies at the calyx synapse have shown only marginal changes in the presynaptic AP waveform or presynaptic Ca2+ influx during PTP.
source: However, studies at the calyx synapse have shown only marginal changes in the presynaptic AP waveform or presynaptic Ca2+ influx during PTP (Habets and Borst, 2006; Korogod et al., 2007), or during phorbol ester mediated potentiation of transmitter release (Lou et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Studies at the calyx synapse have shown only marginal changes in the presynaptic AP waveform or presynaptic Ca2+ influx during phorbol ester mediated potentiation of transmitter release.
source: However, studies at the calyx synapse have shown only marginal changes in the presynaptic AP waveform or presynaptic Ca2+ influx during PTP (Habets and Borst, 2006; Korogod et al., 2007), or during phorbol ester mediated potentiation of transmitter release (Lou et al., 2005, 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Munc18-1 is a member of the Sec1/Munc18 family of proteins essential for membrane fusion from yeast to mammals.
source: Munc18-1 is a member of the Sec1/Munc18 family of proteins essential for membrane fusion from yeast to mammals (Verhage et al., 2000; Südhof and Rothman, 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies and represents established knowledge.

claim: Constitutive genetic deletion of Munc18-1 in mice is lethal at the late embryo stage.
source: Since constitutive genetic deletion of Munc18-1 in mice is lethal at the late embryo stage (Verhage et al., 2000), we used Munc18-1lox/lox mice (Heeroma et al., 2004) and recombined the loxP sites using virus-mediated Cre expression.
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous genetic study.

claim: DAG can activate both protein kinase-C and Munc13-1.
source: A second messenger with a centrally important role in presynaptic plasticity is diacylglycerol (DAG), which can activate both protein kinase-C and Munc13-1 (Lackner et al., 1999; Rhee et al., 2002; Wierda et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: During augmentation, activation of the presynaptic protein Munc13-1 either by DAG or by Ca2+/Calmodulin results in increased vesicle priming.
source: During augmentation, activation of the presynaptic protein Munc13-1 either by DAG or by Ca2+/Calmodulin results in increased vesicle priming (Rosenmund et al., 2002; Junge et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylated Munc18-1 has a reduced binding affinity for Syntaxin.
source: An early study showed that the phosphorylated Munc18-1 has a reduced binding affinity for Syntaxin (Fujita et al., 1996); thus, PKC phosphorylation could aid in the transition from a binary Munc18-1/Syntaxin complex to incorporation into SNARE complexes.
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: Munc18-1 stimulates SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion in a reconstituted system by binding to the partially assembled SNARE complex.
source: However, it was shown later that Munc18-1 also binds to the SNARE complex (Dulubova et al., 2007), and stimulates SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion in a reconstituted system, by binding to the partially assembled SNARE complex (Shen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.

claim: Munc13-1 is present in the complex with Munc18-1 at partially formed SNARE complexes.
source: Therefore, Munc18-1 likely remains present at the partially formed SNARE complexes of docked and readily releasable vesicles; interestingly, Munc13-1 is also present in this complex (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on a citation to a previous study.
